concepts.title: 1–2. Financial Needs of a Business and Classification of Financial Sources
understand: **Three financial needs (§1).** (i) ==Long-term financial needs: funds required for a period exceeding 5–10 years== — investment in plant, machinery, land, buildings; funds for **permanent or hard-core working capital** should also come from long-term sources. (ii) ==Medium-term needs: exceeding one year but not exceeding 5 years== — stores and spares, critical spares, tools, dies, moulds. (iii) ==Short-term needs: to finance current assets== (stock, debtors, cash), i.e. working capital; they arise for a period **not exceeding one accounting year**.

==Basic principle for funding: short-term needs from short-term sources, medium-term needs from medium-term sources and long-term needs from long-term sources.== The method of raising funds is decided with reference to the period for which funds are required.

The general rule can change with the **nature and level of operation of the borrower** and the **stage of development** of the business: Early stage — high uncertainty — **equity, mainly angel fund**; high to moderate uncertainty — **equity, venture capital, debt**; growth stage — moderate to low uncertainty — **debt, venture capital, private equity**; stable stage — low uncertainty — **debt**.
**Classification (§2).** Sources are classified in three ways: **(i) based on basic sources, (ii) based on maturity of repayment period, (iii) based on ownership and control**.

**By basic source (§2.1): External sources** — share capital (equity shares, preference shares) and debt or borrowed capital (debentures, loans from financial institutions, others); **Internal sources** — mainly **retained earnings**.

**By maturity (§2.2). Long-term:** share capital/equity shares; preference shares; retained earnings; debentures/bonds of different types; loans from financial institutions; loans from State Financial Corporations; loans from commercial banks; venture capital funding; asset securitisation; international financing such as Euro-issues and foreign currency loans. **Medium-term:** preference shares; debentures/bonds; public/fixed deposits for three years; medium-term loans from commercial banks, financial institutions and State Financial Corporations; lease financing / hire-purchase financing; external commercial borrowings; Euro-issues; foreign currency bonds. **Short-term:** trade credit; accrued expenses and deferred income; short-term loans such as working capital loans from commercial banks; advances received from customers; various short-term provisions.
**By ownership and control (§2.3): Owner's fund** — equity share capital and retained earnings; **Borrowed fund** — debentures, loans from banks, loans from financial institutions and others.
concepts.example: A start-up with an untested product raises angel equity (early stage, high uncertainty); once sales stabilise it borrows from a bank (stable stage, low uncertainty) — exactly the SM's stage-wise table.

expected_questions.question: Explain the three categories of financial needs of a business and the basic principle for funding them.
answer_points: Long-term financial needs: funds for a period exceeding 5–10 years, e.g. plant, machinery, land and buildings; permanent or hard-core working capital should also be financed from long-term sources.
Medium-term financial needs: funds for a period exceeding one year but not exceeding five years, e.g. stores and spares, critical spares, tools, dies and moulds.
Short-term financial needs: funds to finance current assets such as stock, debtors and cash, i.e. working capital, arising for a period not exceeding one accounting year.

Basic principle: short-term needs should be met from short-term sources, medium-term needs from medium-term sources and long-term needs from long-term sources; the method of raising funds is decided by the period for which funds are needed.

The rule flexes with the borrower's level of operation, the stage of development and the nature of business (early stage: equity and angel funds; growth: debt, venture capital, private equity; stable: debt).

concepts.title: 3–3.1 Long-term Sources: Owners' Capital or Equity Capital
understand: Long-term sources are broadly **share capital (equity and preference)** and **debt** (debentures, long-term borrowings, other debt instruments).

**Equity capital (§3.1).** A public limited company raises owner's capital from promoters or the investing public by issuing **ordinary equity shares**. Characteristics: it is a source of **permanent capital**; holders are **equity or ordinary shareholders**; they are practically the **owners** and undertake the **highest risk**; they are entitled to dividends **after the income claims of other stakeholders are satisfied**, and dividend is an **appropriation of profits, not a charge**; on winding up they claim **after all other suppliers of capital**; the **cost of ordinary shares is usually the highest** because their risk is highest; equity also provides **security to other suppliers of funds** (lenders check that the debt-equity ratio can cover the debt). Types include **new issue, rights issue, bonus shares and sweat equity**.

**Advantages of equity shares:** (i) **permanent source** — not redeemable, so no cash outflow on redemption; once issued, shares are tradable and the company is not responsible for investors' cash flows; (ii) it **increases the financial base** and so the **borrowing power** of the company (debt then raises EPS and share price); (iii) the company is **not legally obliged to pay dividends**, so in uncertain times payments can be reduced or suspended; (iv) capital can be increased further through a **rights issue**.

**Disadvantages of equity shares:** (i) investors find ordinary shares **riskier** because of uncertain dividends and capital gains; (ii) a new issue **reduces EPS** of existing shareholders unless profits rise proportionately; (iii) a new issue can **reduce the ownership and control** of existing shareholders.
**Retained earnings (§3.3, covered with the next block)** belong to ordinary shareholders and increase net worth.
concepts.example: A profitable company funds a new plant with a rights issue: no fixed obligation and no dilution to outsiders, but EPS falls until the plant earns.

concepts.title: 3.2–3.3 Preference Share Capital and Retained Earnings
understand: **Preference shares (§3.2)** are a special kind of share whose holders enjoy **priority both as to payment of a fixed dividend and repayment of capital on winding up**. Characteristics: long-term funds can be raised through a **public issue**; such shares are **normally cumulative** (dividend of a loss year is carried over until there are adequate profits); the **rate of dividend is normally higher than the rate of interest** on debentures and loans; most carry a **stipulated period** and must be repaid at its end.

==Preference share capital is a hybrid form of financing: like equity because preference dividend, like equity dividend, is not a tax-deductible payment; like debt because the rate of dividend is fixed.==

**Cumulative Convertible Preference Shares (CCPs)** may be offered, carrying a cumulative dividend for a period of, say, three years, after which they are converted into equity; these suit projects with a **long gestation period**. Preference capital may be **redeemed at a pre-decided future date or earlier out of profits**, letting promoters withdraw capital from a now self-sufficient company and reinvest it.

**Types of preference shares (SM table):** **Cumulative** — arrear dividend will accumulate; **Non-cumulative** — no right to arrear dividend; **Redeemable** — redemption should be done; **Participating** — can participate in the surplus remaining after payment to equity shareholders; **Non-participating** — cannot participate in the surplus after payment of a fixed rate of dividend; **Convertible** — option of converting into equity shares.

**Advantages of preference shares:** (i) **no dilution in EPS** on an enlarged capital base (equity issue would reduce EPS and affect market perception); (ii) **leverage advantage**, as it bears a fixed charge, while non-payment of preference dividend does not force the company into liquidation; (iii) **no risk of takeover**, since preference shareholders have no voting rights except where dividends are in arrears; (iv) preference dividends are **fixed and pre-decided**, so holders cannot share surplus profits (except participating shares); (v) capital can be **redeemed** after a specified period.

**Disadvantages:** (i) preference dividend is **not tax deductible**, so it gives no tax shield and preference shares are **costlier than debt such as debentures**; (ii) preference dividends are **cumulative**, so unpaid dividends accumulate and until they are paid no dividend can be paid to ordinary shareholders, which can seriously impair the company's reputation.

**Equity vs preference shares (SM table):** dividend payment — equity dividend is paid after preference dividend; rate of dividend — fluctuating vs fixed; convertibility — equity not convertible, preference convertible; voting rights — equity shareholders enjoy full voting rights, preference shareholders have very limited voting rights.

**Retained earnings (§3.3).** Long-term funds may be provided by **accumulating profits and ploughing them back**. Such funds **belong to the ordinary shareholders** and increase the **net worth**. A public limited company must plough back a reasonable amount every year, keeping in view legal requirements and its expansion plans. These funds entail **almost no risk** and the **control of present owners is not diluted**. The decision to plough back depends on the **rate of return generated by the company versus the expected cost of equity** (discussed in the dividend chapter).

concepts.title: 3.4–3.5 Debentures and Bonds
concepts.evidence: PYQ 2 (Sep 2024 Q4(a), Sep 2025 Q4(b)) · MTP 2 (Apr 2025, Aug 2026)
understand: **Debentures (§3.4).** Loans can be raised from the public by issuing debentures or bonds. Characteristics: issued in **denominations of ₹100 to ₹1,000** carrying different rates of interest; normally issued on the basis of a **debenture trust deed** listing the terms; they are instruments for raising **long-term debt capital**; the **maturity period normally varies from 3 to 10 years** (longer for high-gestation projects); they are **either secured or unsecured**; they **may or may not be listed**; the **cost of capital raised is quite low** since interest is charged as an expense before tax; from the investor's point of view they are **more attractive than preference shares** because interest is payable whether or not the company makes profits.

**By convertibility:** (i) **Non-convertible** — no conversion feature, repayable on maturity; (ii) **Fully convertible** — converted into equity as per terms of issue; interest rates are generally **lower** than on non-convertible debentures because of the conversion attraction; (iii) **Partly convertible** — carries features of both.

**Other types (SM table):** **Bearer** — transferable like negotiable instruments; **Registered** — interest payable to the registered person; **Mortgage** — secured by a charge on asset(s); **Naked or simple** — unsecured; **Redeemable** — repaid after a certain period; **Non-redeemable** — not repayable.

**Advantages of debentures:** (i) **cost is much lower** than preference or equity capital as interest is tax-deductible, and investors consider debentures safer so require a lower return; (ii) **no dilution of control**; (iii) in a **period of rising prices** the fixed monetary outgo decreases in real terms.

**Disadvantages:** (i) interest and repayment of principal are **obligatory payments**; (ii) **protective covenants** may be restrictive; (iii) debenture financing **enhances financial risk**; (iv) a **large cash outflow** is needed at maturity.

Public issue of debentures and private placement to mutual funds require the issue to be **rated by a credit rating agency** such as **CRISIL**; the rating evaluates track record, profitability, debt servicing capacity, credit worthiness and perceived risk of lending.

**Preference shares vs debentures (SM table):** ownership — preference share capital is a special kind of share while a debenture is a type of loan raised from the public; payment — preference shareholders enjoy priority for a fixed dividend and repayment on winding up, while debentures carry a fixed percentage of interest; nature — preference shares are a hybrid form of financing, debentures are instruments for long-term capital with a fixed maturity.

**Bonds (§3.5).** A bond is a **fixed income security created to raise funds**, raised through **public issue or private placement**. By call feature: **callable bonds** — a call option gives the **issuer the right to redeem before maturity at a predetermined call price** (generally at a premium); **puttable bonds** — give the **investor a put option, i.e. the right to sell the bond back** to the company before maturity.

**Foreign bonds (SM table).** **FCCB** — very low interest rate; issuer gets foreign currency cheaply; risk that the issuer may not have money on redemption. **Plain vanilla bond** — principal plus interest, no options, issued as a discounted or coupon-bearing bond. **Convertible FRN** — holder can convert into a longer-term debt security with a specified coupon; protects against falling interest rates; the long-term security can be sold for profit; capital gain is not applicable. **Drop lock bond** — a floating rate note that **automatically converts into a fixed rate bond if the rate falls below a predetermined level**, and the new fixed rate stays till maturity (a short option structure, unlike the convertible FRN which is a long option structure). **Variable rate demand obligations** — a floating rate note with nominal maturity whose holder can sell it back to the trustee at par plus accrued interest, so it is more liquid. **Yield curve note (YCN)** — a structured debt security whose yield **increases when interest rates decline** and vice versa; used to hedge interest rates; works like an inverse floater. **Euro bond** — issued or traded in a country using a currency other than the one in which it is denominated; issued by multinationals (a British company issuing in Germany denominated in US dollars); the prefix 'euro' has nothing to do with the euro currency. **Emerging market bond** — issued by developing countries, higher yields than US corporate and Treasury bonds, credit default swaps used for protection, higher risks.

**Indian bonds:** **Masala bond** — Indian name for a **rupee-denominated bond that Indian corporate borrowers sell to investors in overseas markets**, issued outside India but denominated in rupees (NTPC raised ₹2,000 crore in 2016). **Municipal bonds** — finance urban infrastructure (Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation issued Asia's first municipal bond, ₹100 crore, for a water supply project). **Government or Treasury bonds** — issued by the Government of India, RBI, state governments or government departments.

official_questions.question: Discuss any two advantages and two disadvantages of raising finance by issue of debentures.
answer_points: **Advantages:** (i) the cost of debentures is much lower than the cost of preference or equity capital as interest is tax-deductible; investors also consider debenture investment safer than equity or preference investment and hence may require a lower return.
(ii) Debenture financing does not result in dilution of control.
(iii) In a period of rising prices, debenture issue is advantageous: the fixed monetary outgo decreases in real terms as the price level increases.
**Disadvantages:** (i) debenture interest and repayment of principal are obligatory payments.
(ii) The protective covenants associated with a debenture issue may be restrictive.
(iii) Debenture financing enhances the financial risk associated with the firm.
(iv) Since debentures must be paid at maturity, a large cash outflow is needed at that time.

official_questions.question: Explain in brief the following types of bonds: (i) callable bonds, (ii) puttable bonds, (iii) masala bonds, (iv) drop lock bonds.
answer_points: **Callable bonds:** a callable bond has a call option which gives the issuer the right to redeem the bond before maturity at a predetermined price known as the call price (generally at a premium).
**Puttable bonds:** puttable bonds give the investor a put option, i.e. the right to sell the bond back to the company before maturity.
**Masala bonds:** masala (meaning spice) bond is an Indian name used for a rupee-denominated bond that Indian corporate borrowers can sell to investors in overseas markets.

**Drop lock bond:** it is a floating rate note with a normal floating rate; the floating rate bond is automatically converted into a fixed rate bond if the interest rate falls below a predetermined level, and the new fixed rate stays till the bond reaches maturity.
also_asked_as: MTP-S26-S2-FQ4c (explain callable bonds and puttable bonds, 2 marks)

official_questions.question: Explain any four features of debentures or bonds.
answer_points: **Face value:** debentures or bonds are denominated with a value called the face value; interest is calculated on it (e.g. a 9% non-convertible debenture of ₹100 carries interest at 9% of ₹100).

**Interest (coupon) rate:** each debenture bears a fixed interest (coupon) rate, except zero coupon and deep discount bonds; it is applied to face value and paid periodically (annually, semi-annually etc.).
**Maturity period:** debentures or bonds have a fixed maturity period for redemption; for irredeemable debentures the maturity period is not defined and is taken as infinite.
**Redemption value:** redeemable debentures are redeemed on the specified maturity date; based on debt covenants the redemption value is determined and may differ from face value.
**Benefit of tax shield:** interest paid to debenture holders is allowed as an expense for corporate tax, so it saves tax — this saving is known as the tax shield.
official_questions.conclusion: Any four of these five features earn the marks.

expected_questions.question: Explain the following: (i) Euro bond, (ii) yield curve note, (iii) emerging market bond, (iv) plain vanilla bond.
answer_points: **Euro bond:** issued or traded in a country using a currency other than the one in which the bond is denominated; issued by multinational corporations (e.g. a British company issuing a bond in Germany denominated in US dollars). The prefix 'euro' has nothing to do with the euro currency.

**Yield curve note (YCN):** a structured debt security whose yield increases when prevailing interest rates decline and decreases when they rise; used to hedge interest rate risk and works like an inverse floater.

**Emerging market bond:** a debt instrument issued by developing countries; provides higher yields than US corporate and Treasury bonds; credit default swaps are used to protect bondholders against default; it carries higher risks than domestic debt instruments.
**Plain vanilla bond:** the issuer pays the principal along with the interest rate; it has no options and may be issued as a discounted bond or a coupon-bearing bond.

concepts.title: 3.6–3.7 Loans from Financial Institutions and Commercial Banks (including Bridge Finance)
understand: **Loans from financial institutions (§3.6).** The study material lists the institutions in two tables. **National:** Industrial Finance Corporation of India (**IFCI**), 1918, converted into a public company; **State Financial Corporations (SFCs)**, 1951; Industrial Development Bank of India (**IDBI**), 1954, converted into a bank; National Industrial Development Corporation (**NIDC**), 1954; Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation of India (**ICICI**), 1955, converted into a bank and privatised; Life Insurance Corporation of India (**LIC**), 1956; Unit Trust of India (**UTI**), 1964; Industrial Reconstruction Bank of India (**IRBI**), 1971. **International:** The World Bank / International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (**IBRD**), 1944; The International Finance Corporation (**IFC**), 1956; Asian Development Bank (**ADB**), 1966.

**Loans from commercial banks (§3.7).** The **primary role of commercial banks is to cater to the short-term requirements of industry**, but banks have started taking an interest in long-term financing in two ways: (a) they provide **long-term loans for expansion or setting up of new units**, repayment scheduled over a long period, the liquidity of such loans depending on the **anticipated income of the borrowers**; (b) as part of long-term funding they also fund the **long-term working capital requirement — the working capital term loan (WCTL)** — being that portion of working capital which is **always required (the minimum level) and is not impacted by seasonal requirement**.

==**Bridge finance** refers to loans taken by a company normally from commercial banks **for a short period because of pending disbursement of loans sanctioned by financial institutions**.== Though short-term in nature, it is an important step in facilitating the long-term loan, so the study material discusses it with long-term sources.

Normally it takes time for financial institutions to disburse loans. Once the loans are approved by the term lending institutions, companies, **in order not to lose further time in starting their projects**, arrange short-term loans from commercial banks.

**The bridge loans are repaid or adjusted out of the term loans as and when disbursed** by the concerned institutions. They are **normally secured by hypothecating movable assets, personal guarantees and demand promissory notes**. Generally, the **rate of interest on bridge finance is higher** than on term loans.
concepts.example: A company's ₹50 crore term loan is sanctioned in March but will be released in July. It borrows ₹10 crore from its bank in April against hypothecation of plant and a promissory note, starts construction, and squares off the bank loan when the institution disburses.

concepts.title: 4. Venture Capital Financing: Meaning, Characteristics and Methods
understand: **Meaning (§4.1).** ==Venture capital financing refers to financing of a **new high-risky venture** promoted by **qualified entrepreneurs who lack experience and funds** to give shape to their ideas.== In a broad sense, under venture capital financing, **venture capitalists make investment to purchase equity or debt securities from inexperienced entrepreneurs who undertake highly risky ventures with potential to succeed in future**.

**Characteristics (§4.2).** (i) It is **basically an equity finance in new companies**. (ii) It can be viewed as a **long-term investment in growth-oriented small or medium firms**. (iii) Apart from providing funds, the investor also **provides support in the form of sales strategy, business networking and management expertise**, enabling the growth of the entrepreneur.

**Methods (§4.3) — four methods.** **(i) Equity financing:** venture capital undertakings generally require funds for a longer period but may not be able to provide returns to investors during the initial stages, so venture capital finance is generally provided by way of **equity share capital**. ==The equity contribution of the venture capital firm **does not exceed 49% of the total equity capital** of the venture capital undertaking, so that the effective control and ownership remains with the entrepreneur.==

**(ii) Conditional loan:** repayable in the form of a **royalty after the venture is able to generate sales**. **No interest is paid** on such loans. In India venture capital financiers charge **royalty ranging between 2 and 15 per cent**; the actual rate depends on other factors such as gestation period, cash flow patterns, risk and other factors of the enterprise. Some financiers give the enterprise a **choice of paying a high rate of interest (which could be well above 20 per cent) instead of royalty on sales** once it becomes commercially sound.

**(iii) Income note:** a **hybrid security combining the features of both a conventional loan and a conditional loan**. The entrepreneur has to pay **both interest and royalty on sales, but at substantially low rates**. IDBI's VCF provides funding equal to **80 – 87.50% of the project cost** for commercial application of indigenous technology.

**(iv) Participating debenture:** such security **carries charges in three phases** — in the **start-up phase no interest is charged**; in the **next stage a low rate of interest is charged up to a particular level of operation**; **after that, a high rate of interest is required to be paid**.
concepts.example: A venture fund puts ₹4 crore into a start-up's ₹10 crore equity (40%, within the 49% cap), takes a board seat and helps build the sales network — exactly the SM's third characteristic.

concepts.title: 5. Debt Securitisation
concepts.evidence: MTP 2 (May 2025 Series I, Sep 2026 Series I)
understand: ==**Securitisation is a process in which illiquid assets are pooled into marketable securities that can be sold to investors.**== The process leads to the creation of financial instruments that **represent ownership interest in, or are secured by, a segregated income-producing asset or pool of assets**. These assets are **generally secured by personal or real property such as automobiles, real estate or equipment loans, but in some cases are unsecured**.

**The study material's example.** A finance company has given a large number of car loans and needs more money to give further loans. One way would be to sell all the existing loans, but **in the absence of a liquid secondary market for individual car loans this is not feasible**. The practical option is debt securitisation: the finance company **sells its existing car loans to a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV)**; the SPV pays the company, which continues to lend with this money, and the SPV **pools these loans and converts them into marketable securities** issued to investors.

So the process helps the finance company **raise funds and get the loans off its balance sheet**, and the funds help it disburse further loans. It also benefits investors by creating a **liquid investment in a diversified pool of car loans**, an attractive option compared with other fixed-income instruments. The whole process is carried out in such a way that the **original debtors may not be aware of the transaction** — they continue making payments as before, but these payments now go to the new investors.

**The three-step process ICAI expects in the answer.** **(i) The origination function** — a borrower seeks a loan from a finance company or bank; the creditworthiness of the borrower is evaluated and a contract is entered into with a repayment schedule structured over the life of the loan. **(ii) The pooling function** — similar loans or receivables are clubbed together to create an underlying pool of assets; the pool is **transferred in favour of the Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV), which acts as a trustee for investors**. **(iii) The securitisation function** — the SPV structures and issues securities on the basis of the asset pool; the securities carry a **coupon and expected maturity** and can be **asset-based or mortgage-based**; they are generally sold to investors through **merchant bankers**, the investors being **pension funds, mutual funds and insurance funds**.

==The process of securitisation is generally **without recourse**: investors bear the credit risk, and the issuer is under an obligation to pay investors **only if the cash flows are received by him from the collateral**.== The benefit to the originator is that **assets are shifted off the balance sheet**, giving the originator recourse to **off-balance-sheet funding**.

Debt securitisation is also described as a **method of recycling of funds**, especially beneficial to **financial intermediaries to support lending volumes**: assets generating steady cash flows are packaged together and market securities are issued against the asset pool — for example **housing finance, auto loans and credit card receivables**.
concepts.example: A housing finance company pools ₹500 crore of home loans, transfers them to an SPV, and the SPV issues mortgage-backed securities to a pension fund. The company gets ₹500 crore back to lend again; the borrowers keep paying their EMIs, now for the investors.

official_questions.question: Explain debt securitisation and describe its process.
answer_points: **Debt securitisation** is a method of recycling of funds. It is especially beneficial to financial intermediaries to support the lending volumes. Assets generating steady cash flows are packaged together and, against this asset pool, market securities can be issued — for example housing finance, auto loans and credit card receivables.

**(i) The origination function:** a borrower seeks a loan from a finance company or bank; the creditworthiness of the borrower is evaluated and a contract is entered into with a repayment schedule structured over the life of the loan.

**(ii) The pooling function:** similar loans or receivables are clubbed together to create an underlying pool of assets; the pool is transferred in favour of the Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV), which acts as a trustee for investors.

**(iii) The securitisation function:** the SPV will structure and issue securities on the basis of the asset pool; the securities carry a coupon and expected maturity and can be asset-based or mortgage-based, and are generally sold to investors through merchant bankers. Investors are pension funds, mutual funds and insurance funds.

The process of securitisation is generally without recourse, i.e. investors bear the credit risk and the issuer is under an obligation to pay investors only if the cash flows are received by him from the collateral. The benefit to the originator is that assets are shifted off the balance sheet, giving the originator recourse to off-balance-sheet funding.
official_questions.conclusion: Meaning, three functions and the without-recourse close — that is the full 4 marks.

The finance company sells its existing car loans to a Special Purpose Vehicle; the SPV pays the company, which continues to lend with this money, and the SPV pools the loans and converts them into marketable securities issued to investors.

The company thus raises funds and gets the loans off its balance sheet, obtaining off-balance-sheet funding; investors get a liquid investment in a diversified pool of car loans, an attractive alternative to other fixed-income instruments.
The original borrowers may not even be aware of the transaction; they continue making payments as before, which now flow to the new investors.
The process is generally without recourse, so the investors bear the credit risk; the issuer is obliged to pay investors only if the cash flows are received from the collateral.

concepts.title: 6–6.1 Lease Financing: Operating and Financial Leases
understand: **Meaning (§6).** ==Leasing is a **general contract between the owner and the user of the asset over a specified period of time**.== The asset is **purchased initially by the lessor (leasing company)** and thereafter **leased to the user (lessee company)**, which pays a **specified rent at periodical intervals**. Leasing is an **alternative to the purchase of an asset out of own or borrowed funds**. Moreover, **lease finance can be arranged much faster than term loans from financial institutions**.
**Two broad categories (§6.1): (a) operating lease and (b) financial lease.**

**(a) Operating lease.** The **right to use the asset is given by the lessor to the lessee**, but the **ownership right remains with the lessor**. The lessee gives a **fixed amount of periodic lease rentals**. The **lessor bears the insurance, maintenance and repair costs** of the asset. The **lease period is short**, so the lessor **may not be able to recover the cost of the asset during the initial lease period and tends to lease the asset to more than one lessee**. Normally these are **callable leases and are cancellable with proper notice**. The **term is shorter than the asset's economic life**; the lessee is obliged to make payment until lease expiration, which approaches the useful life of the asset. It is particularly attractive to companies that **continually update or replace equipment** and want to use equipment without ownership, returning it at lease end and **avoiding technological obsolescence**.

**(b) Financial lease.** In contrast, a financial lease is **long term in nature and non-cancellable** — the lessee cannot terminate the lease agreement subsequently — so the **period of lease is generally the full economic life of the leased asset**. It can be regarded as **any leasing arrangement that is to finance the use of equipment for the major part of its useful life**. The **lessee has the right to use the equipment while the lessor retains legal title**, and the **lessee has to bear the insurance, maintenance and other related costs**. It is **also called a capital lease, which is nothing but a loan in disguise**. A financial lease is a **contract involving payments over an obligatory period of specified sums sufficient in total to amortise the capital outlay of the lessor and give some profit**.

**The SM's five-point comparison.** (1) In a financial lease the **risk and reward incident to ownership pass to the lessee**, the lessor remaining only the legal owner; in an operating lease the lessee is only provided the use of the asset and **risk incident to ownership belongs wholly to the lessor**. (2) In a financial lease the **lessee bears the risk of obsolescence**; in an operating lease the **lessor** bears it. (3) In a financial lease the lessor is **interested in his rentals and not in the asset** — he must get his principal back with interest — so the lease is **non-cancellable by either party**; in an operating lease the lessor has no difficulty leasing the same asset to another willing lessee, so the lease is **kept cancellable by the lessor**. (4) In a financial lease the lessor **enters into the transaction only as financier** and **does not bear the cost of repairs, maintenance or operations**; in an operating lease **usually the lessor bears** those costs. (5) A financial lease is **usually full payout** — the single lease repays the cost of the asset together with interest; an operating lease is **usually non-payout**, since the lessor expects to lease the same asset over and over again to several users.
concepts.example: A printer taken for two years with the vendor servicing it and the option to return it early is an operating lease; a machine taken for its whole ten-year life on a non-cancellable contract, with the user paying insurance and repairs, is a financial lease.

concepts.title: 6.2 Other Types of Leases
concepts.evidence: PYQ 1 (Sep 2024 Q4(c)) · MTP 4 (Sep 2024 S2, May 2025 S2, Jan 2026 S2, Sep 2026 S1)
understand: **(a) Sale and lease back.** ==The **owner of an asset sells the asset to a party (the buyer), who in turn leases back the same asset to the owner** in consideration of lease rentals.== Under this arrangement the **asset is not physically exchanged — it all happens in records only**. The main advantage is that the **lessee can satisfy himself completely regarding the quality of the asset** and, after possession of the asset, convert the sale into a lease agreement. In this transaction the **seller assumes the role of lessee** (the same asset he sold comes back to him as a lease) and the **buyer assumes the role of lessor**. So the **seller gets the agreed selling price and the buyer gets the lease rentals**.

**(b) Leveraged lease.** ==Under this lease a **third party is involved besides the lessor and the lessee**.== The **lessor borrows a part of the purchase cost (say 80%) of the asset from the third party, i.e. the lender**, and the asset so purchased is **held as security against the loan**. The **lender is paid off from the lease rentals directly by the lessee**, and the **surplus after meeting the claims of the lender goes to the lessor**. The **lessor is entitled to claim depreciation allowance**.

**(c) Sales-aid lease.** Where the **lessor enters into a tie-up with a manufacturer for marketing the latter's product through his own leasing operations**, it is called a sales-aid lease. In consideration of the aid in sales, the **manufacturer may grant either credit or a commission to the lessor**. Thus the **lessor earns from both sources — from the lessee as well as from the manufacturer**.

**(d) Close-ended and open-ended leases.** In the **close-ended lease, the assets get transferred to the lessor at the end of the lease**, and the **risk of obsolescence, residual value etc. remain with the lessor**, being the legal owner of the asset. In the **open-ended lease, the lessee has the option of purchasing the asset at the end of the lease period**.

**The study material's closing note on leasing.** In recent years leasing has become a popular source of financing in India. From the **lessee's point of view, leasing eliminates immediate cash outflow, and the lease rentals can be deducted for computing total income under the Income-tax Act**. As against this, **buying has the advantages of depreciation allowance (including additional depreciation) and interest on borrowed capital being tax-deductible**. So **an evaluation of the two alternatives has to be made** before deciding. Practical problems of lease financing are covered at the Final level in Financial Services and Capital Markets.

concepts.title: 7. Short-term Sources of Finance (including Export Finance)
concepts.evidence: PYQ 1 (May 2026 Q4(b)) · MTP 1 (Mar 2024 Series I, MCQ)
understand: The study material lists **ten short-term sources**. **(i) Trade credit** — credit granted by suppliers of goods as an incident of sale; usual duration **15 to 90 days**; it **generates automatically** in the course of business; it can be an **'open account' or 'bills payable'**; it is preferred because it is **without any explicit cost** and keeps rotating while the business is a going concern, and it **enhances automatically with the increase in the volume of business**.

**(ii) Accrued expenses and deferred (unearned) income** — accrued expenses are liabilities for services already received such as **wages, taxes, interest and dividends**, arising out of day-to-day activities and hence a **spontaneous source**; deferred income is **funds received in lieu of goods and services to be provided in the future**, which increase liquidity and are also a spontaneous source. **(iii) Advances from customers** — manufacturers and contractors producing costly goods over a long manufacturing period demand advance money when accepting orders; this is a **cost-free source of finance**.

**(iv) Commercial paper** — an **unsecured money market instrument issued in the form of a promissory note**; the RBI introduced the scheme in **1989** to let highly rated corporate borrowers diversify their short-term borrowings; **Primary Dealers and All India Financial Institutions** were later also allowed to issue it. ==Commercial papers are issued in **denominations of ₹5 lakh or multiples thereof**, and the interest rate is generally **linked to the yield on the one-year government bond**.== All eligible issuers must obtain a **credit rating from CRISIL, ICRA, CARE, FITCH Ratings India or any other agency specified by the RBI**.

**(v) Treasury bills** — a class of **Central Government securities** issued by the Government of India to meet short-term borrowing requirements, with **maturities ranging between 14 and 364 days**. **(vi) Certificates of deposit** — a document of title similar to a time deposit receipt with a **fixed maturity date of not less than 7 days up to a maximum of one year**, issued by a bank, except that **no interest rate is prescribed**; the advantage is that the **banker is not required to encash the deposit before maturity** while the **investor is assured of liquidity because he can sell the CD in the secondary market**.

**(vii) Bank advances.** Facilities provided by banks: **short-term loans** — the entire advance is disbursed at one time against securities like shares, government securities, life insurance policies and fixed deposit receipts; **overdraft** — customers may withdraw in excess of the credit balance in the current account up to a fixed limit, repayable on demand but generally continued by annual renewals, with **interest charged on daily balances**; **clean overdrafts** — entertained only from parties which are financially sound and of good repute, as the bank relies on the **personal security of the borrower** and has no tangible security, so banks take guarantees and grant them only for a short period; **cash credit** — an advance up to a certain limit where the customer **draws only to the extent of his requirements and deposits surplus funds**, with **interest charged on the amount actually availed** and limits sanctioned **against tradable goods by way of pledge or hypothecation**; **advances against goods** — safe and liquid because goods are in constant demand, charged by pledge or hypothecation, 'goods' including all forms of movables; **bills purchased or discounted** — advances against clean or documentary bills, where in actual practice the **bank holds the bills only as security for the advance**.

**(viii) Financing of export trade by banks.** Commercial banks provide short-term export finance mainly by **pre-shipment and post-shipment credit**, granted in **rupees as well as foreign currency**. RBI measures include rationalisation and liberalisation of export credit interest rates, flexibility in repayment or prepayment of pre-shipment credit, a special financial package for large-value exporters, export finance for agricultural exports and the **Gold Card Scheme** for exporters.

**Pre-shipment finance** generally takes the form of a **packing credit facility**: ==an advance extended by banks to an exporter for the purpose of **buying, manufacturing, processing, packing and shipping goods to overseas buyers**.== Any exporter with a **firm export order or an irrevocable letter of credit opened in his favour** can approach a bank. ==The advance is **required to be liquidated within 180 days** from the date of its commencement by negotiation of export bills or receipt of export proceeds in an approved manner== — so packing credit is essentially a short-term advance. **Types of packing credit:** **clean packing credit** (against a firm export order or letter of credit, without any charge or control over raw material or finished goods, with a suitable margin and ECGC cover obtained by the bank); **packing credit against hypothecation of goods** (goods hypothecated with a stipulated margin, with stock statements submitted every fortnight or on movement of stocks); **packing credit against pledge of goods** (finished goods pledged with approved clearing agents, possession lying with the bank under its lock and key); **E.C.G.C. guarantee** (any loan for manufacture, processing, purchasing or packing of goods for export against a firm order qualifies for the packing credit guarantee); and **forward exchange contract** (where the export bill is in foreign currency, the exporter should enter into a forward exchange contract with the bank, avoiding the risk of a change in the rate of exchange).

**Post-shipment finance** takes four forms: **(a) purchase or discounting of documentary export bills** — finance by purchasing export bills drawn payable at sight or discounting usance export bills covering confirmed sales and backed by documents of title such as bills of lading, post parcel receipts or air consignment notes; **(b) E.C.G.C. guarantee** — post-shipment finance through purchase, negotiation or discount of an export bill against an order qualifies for the post-shipment export credit guarantee, provided the exporter obtains a shipment or contracts risk policy of ECGC covering both political and commercial risks, with the Corporation fixing credit limits for individual exporters; **(c) advance against export bills sent for collection** — taking into account the creditworthiness of the party, nature of goods exported, usance and standing of the drawee; **(d) advance against duty drawbacks, cash subsidy etc.** — to finance export losses, advanced against duty drawback and cash subsidy receivable against export performance; such advances are of a **clean nature**, so necessary precautions must be exercised. ==A post-shipment advance is also **required to be liquidated within 180 days from the date of shipment**.==

**(ix) Inter-corporate deposits** — companies can borrow for a short period, **say 6 months, from other companies which have surplus liquidity**; the rate of interest varies with the amount and time period. **(x) Public deposits** — a very important source of short-term and medium-term finance, particularly due to credit squeeze by the RBI. ==A company can accept public deposits subject to RBI stipulations **up to a maximum of 35 per cent of its paid-up capital and reserves**, for a period of **six months to three years**.== Public deposits are **unsecured loans**; they **should not be used for acquiring fixed assets** since they must be repaid within three years, and are mainly used to finance **working capital requirements**.

official_questions.question: An Indian exporter has shipped goods to a foreign buyer, but the export proceeds are yet to be realised. He approaches the bank for immediate finance assistance. (i) Identify the type of finance involved. (ii) Explain any three forms of such type of finance.
answer_points: **(i) The finance involved is post-shipment finance**, extended by commercial banks after the shipment of goods.

**(a) Purchase or discounting of documentary export bills:** finance is provided to exporters by purchasing export bills drawn payable at sight, or by discounting usance export bills covering confirmed sales and backed by documents including documents of title to goods such as a bill of lading, post parcel receipts or air consignment notes.

**(b) E.C.G.C. guarantee:** post-shipment finance given to an exporter by a bank through purchase, negotiation or discount of an export bill against an order qualifies for the post-shipment export credit guarantee. The exporter should obtain a shipment or contracts risk policy of ECGC; banks insist on a contracts shipments (comprehensive risks) policy covering both political and commercial risks. On acceptance of the policy the Corporation fixes credit limits for individual exporters, and its liability is limited to the extent of that limit irrespective of the amount of the policy.

**(c) Advance against export bills sent for collection:** finance is provided by banks by way of advance against export bills forwarded through them for collection, taking into account the creditworthiness of the party, nature of goods exported, usance, standing of the drawee etc.

**(d) Advance against duty drawbacks, cash subsidy etc.:** to finance export losses sustained by exporters, banks advance against duty drawback, cash subsidy etc. receivable against export performance; such advances are of a clean nature, hence necessary precautions should be exercised.

official_questions.question: What do you understand by spontaneous sources of finance, and explain its sources of finance?
answer_points: **Spontaneous sources of finance are those which naturally arise in the course of business operations.** Trade credit, credit from employees and credit from suppliers of services are examples.

**Trade credit** is a spontaneous source of finance which is normally extended to the purchaser organisation by the sellers or service providers. It **contributes about one-third of the total short-term requirements**.
**Bills payable:** here the purchaser has to give a written promise to pay the amount of the bill or invoice, either on demand or at a fixed future date, to the seller or the bearer of the note.

**Accrued expenses** represent liabilities the company has to pay for services it has already received — wages, taxes, interest and dividends. They arise out of the day-to-day activities of the company and hence represent a spontaneous source of finance.

**Deferred income** reflects funds received in lieu of goods and services to be provided in the future; since these receipts increase liquidity, they are also an important source of spontaneous finance.
The common thread is that none of these has to be negotiated or arranged: they appear as a by-product of trading, and they **enhance automatically with the increase in the volume of business**.
official_questions.conclusion: Define, then give trade credit, bills payable, accrued expenses and deferred income.

expected_questions.question: Explain packing credit and state its types.
answer_points: Pre-shipment finance generally takes the form of a packing credit facility: an advance extended by banks to an exporter for the purpose of buying, manufacturing, processing, packing and shipping goods to overseas buyers.

Any exporter having at hand a firm export order placed by his foreign buyer, or an irrevocable letter of credit opened in his favour, can approach a bank for packing credit; the advance is required to be liquidated within 180 days from the date of its commencement by negotiation of export bills or receipt of export proceeds in an approved manner, so it is essentially a short-term advance.

**Clean packing credit:** made available only on production of a firm export order or letter of credit, without exercising any charge or control over raw material or finished goods; a suitable margin is maintained and ECGC cover should be obtained by the bank.

**Packing credit against hypothecation of goods:** available where the exporter has a pledgeable interest and the goods are hypothecated to the bank as security with a stipulated margin; stock statements are submitted every fortnight or whenever stocks move.
**Packing credit against pledge of goods:** the exportable finished goods are pledged to the bank with approved clearing agents, the possession lying with the bank under its lock and key.

**E.C.G.C. guarantee and forward exchange contract:** any loan for manufacture, processing, purchasing or packing of goods for export against a firm order qualifies for the packing credit guarantee; and where the export bill is in foreign currency, the exporter should enter into a forward exchange contract with the bank to avoid exchange-rate risk.

understand: **(i) Seed capital assistance.** ==The Seed Capital Assistance scheme is **designed by IDBI for professionally or technically qualified entrepreneurs and/or persons possessing relevant experience, skills and entrepreneurial traits but who lack adequate financial resources**.== All projects eligible for financial assistance from IDBI, directly or indirectly through refinance, are eligible under the scheme. The assistance is **interest free but carries a service charge of one per cent per annum for the first five years and at an increasing rate thereafter**. However, **IDBI has the option to charge interest at such rate as it may determine on the loan if the financial position and profitability of the company so permit** during the currency of the loan. The **repayment schedule is fixed depending upon the repaying capacity of the unit with an initial moratorium of up to five years**.

**(ii) Internal cash accruals.** Existing profit-making companies undertaking an expansion or diversification programme may be permitted to **invest a part of their accumulated reserves or cash profits for creation of capital assets**. The **surplus generated from operations, after meeting all contractual, statutory and working requirements of funds**, is available for further capital expenditure.

**(iii) Unsecured loans.** Typically provided by **promoters to meet the promoters' contribution norm**. They are **subordinate to institutional loans**; the **rate of interest should be less than or equal to the rate on institutional loans**; **interest can be paid only after payment of institutional dues**; they **cannot be repaid without the prior approval of financial institutions**; and they are **considered as part of equity for the purpose of calculating the debt-equity ratio**.

**(iv) Deferred payment guarantee.** Suppliers of machinery often provide a deferred credit facility under which **payment for the purchase of machinery can be made over a period of time**. The **entire cost of the machinery is financed and the company is not required to contribute any amount initially**. Normally the supplier insists that a **bank guarantee should be furnished by the buyer**. Such a facility **does not have a moratorium period for repayment**, hence it is **advisable only for an existing profit-making company**.

**(v) Capital incentives.** Backward area development incentives often determine the **location of a new industrial unit** and usually consist of a **lump sum subsidy and exemption from or deferment of sales tax and octroi duty**; the quantum depends on the **degree of backwardness of the location**. The special capital incentive is a **percentage of the fixed capital investment subject to an overall ceiling** and forms part of the long-term means of finance. However, **the viability of the project must not be dependent on the quantum and availability of incentives** — institutions assess viability per se, without considering the impact of incentives. Incentives are released only after the unit complies with the scheme's requirements, classified into **initial effective steps and final effective steps**.

**Debt instruments listed in this section.** **(vi) Deep discount bonds** — a form of **zero-interest bonds sold at a discounted value**, with the **face value paid on maturity** and **no interest payout during the lock-in period**. **(vii) Secured premium notes** — issued **along with a detachable warrant**, redeemable after a notified period of **say 4 to 7 years**; the warrant must be converted into equity within the period notified by the company. **(viii) Zero interest fully convertible debentures** — fully convertible debentures carrying **no interest**, **compulsorily and automatically converted after a specified period**, holders getting new equity shares at a **predetermined price**; beneficial to the company since no interest is paid, and if the market price is very high investors get shares at a lower rate. **(ix) Zero coupon bonds** — carry **no interest but are sold at a discount**; the **difference between the discounted value and the maturity or face value represents the interest** earned. **(x) Option bonds** — **cumulative and non-cumulative bonds where interest is payable on maturity or periodically**, with a **redemption premium** offered to attract investors. **(xi) Inflation bonds** — bonds in which the **interest rate is adjusted for inflation**, so the investor gets interest free from the effects of inflation (the study material's illustration: at 11 per cent interest and 5 per cent inflation the investor earns 16 per cent). **(xii) Floating rate bonds** — the **interest rate is not fixed and floats with market conditions**; an ideal instrument for the issuer to **hedge against volatility in interest rates**, popular as a money market instrument and issued by institutions such as **IDBI and ICICI**.

**(xiii) High yield bonds (or junk bonds).** ==A junk bond is a bond that is **rated below investment grade by credit rating agencies**. It has a **low credit rating and a high risk of default**. Because of the higher risk, **investors are compensated with higher interest rates, which is why junk bonds are also called high-yield bonds**.==

concepts.title: 9–10. International Financing and Contemporary Sources of Funding
concepts.evidence: PYQ 2 (Jan 2025 Q4(a), May 2024 Q4(c) OR) · RTP 1 (Jan 2026) · MTP 3 (Sep 2024 S1, Mar 2024 S2, Sep 2025 S2)
understand: **Sources of external financing (§9).** **(i) Commercial banks** — extend **Foreign Currency (FC) loans** for international operations and also allow overdrawing over and above the loan amount. **(ii) Development banks** — offer **long and medium term loans including FC loans**; many national agencies offer concessions to foreign companies to invest and to finance exports, e.g. **EXIM Bank of USA**. **(iii) Discounting of trade bills** — a **short-term financing method**, used widely in Europe and Asian countries for both domestic and international business. **(iv) International agencies** — **IFC, IBRD, ADB, IMF** and others. **(v) International capital markets** — foreign currency is available under four main systems: **Euro-currency market, export credit facilities, bond issues and financial institutions**. The **Euro-currency market originated with dollar-denominated bank deposits and loans in Europe, particularly in London**; **Euro-dollar deposits are dollar-denominated time deposits at foreign branches of US banks and some foreign banks**, and funds are made available as loans through **syndicated Euro-credit instruments such as FRNs and FR certificates of deposit**.

**(vi) Financial instruments of the international market.** **External Commercial Borrowings (ECB)** — ==commercial loans (bank loans, buyers' credit, suppliers' credit, securitised instruments such as floating rate notes and fixed rate bonds) **availed from non-resident lenders with a minimum average maturity of 3 years**.== Recognised sources: international banks, international capital markets, multilateral financial institutions such as IFC and ADB, export credit agencies, suppliers of equipment, foreign collaborators and foreign equity holders. ECBs are accessed under **two routes — the Automatic route (no RBI or Government approval needed) and the Approval route**. Companies registered under the Companies Act and NGOs engaged in micro-finance are eligible for the **Automatic route**; financial institutions and banks dealing exclusively in infrastructure or export finance, and those which participated in the textile and steel sector restructuring packages approved by the government, must take the **Approval route**.

**Euro bonds** — debt instruments **not denominated in the currency of the country in which they are issued**, e.g. a **yen note floated in Germany**; generally issued in **bearer form** rather than as registered bonds, so they do not contain the investor's name or country of origin, making them attractive to investors seeking privacy. **Foreign bonds** — debt instruments issued by **foreign corporations or foreign governments**, exposed to **default risk**, denominated in the currency of the country where they are issued; if issued in a currency other than the investor's home currency they are exposed to **exchange rate risks** (example: a British firm placing dollar-denominated bonds in the USA). **Fully hedged bonds** — **eliminate the currency risk by selling in forward markets the entire stream of principal and interest payments**. **Medium Term Notes (MTN)** — for issuers needing frequent financing, where frequent separate issues would be costly; under the MTN programme **several lots of bonds can be issued with different features (different coupon rates, different currencies)**, the **timing of each lot decided in the light of market opportunities**, with the **entire documentation and regulatory approvals taken at one point of time**. **Floating Rate Notes (FRN)** — **issued up to seven years maturity**, with **interest rates adjusted to reflect prevailing exchange rates**; they provide **cheaper money than foreign loans**. **Euro Commercial Papers (ECP)** — **short-term money market instruments with a maturity of less than one year, usually designated in US dollars**.

**Foreign currency option** — the **right (and not the obligation) to buy or sell foreign currency at a certain specified price on or before a specified date**; a hedge against financial and economic risks. **Foreign currency futures** — **obligations (and not the right) to buy or sell a specified foreign currency in the present for settlement at a future date**. **Foreign Euro bonds** — in domestic capital markets the bond issues are known by different names: **Yankee Bonds in the US, Swiss Frances in Switzerland, Samurai Bonds in Tokyo and Bulldogs in the UK**. **Euro convertible bonds** — give the holder an **option to convert into a pre-determined number of equity shares**, usually at a premium; they carry a **fixed rate of interest** and may include a **call option** (issuer may buy the bonds for redemption before maturity) or a **put option** (holder may sell the bonds back at a pre-determined date and price). **Euro convertible zero bonds** — structured as convertible bonds with **no interest payable**, conversion taking place **on maturity at a pre-determined price**, usually a **five-year maturity**, treated as a **deferred equity issue**. **Euro bonds with equity warrants** — carry a **coupon rate determined by market rates**, the **warrants are detachable** and pure bonds are traded at a discount.

**ESG bonds.** ==These bonds **carry a responsibility of the issuer company to prioritise optimal environmental, social and governance factors**; investing in them is considered **socially responsible investing**. ESG bonds can be **project-based — green bonds and social bonds — and target-based — sustainability-linked bonds (SLBs)**.== **Green bonds** are the most popular ESG bonds, issued by a financial, non-financial or public institution, where the **proceeds are used to finance 'green projects'** aimed at positive environmental or climate impact including the cultivation of eco-friendly technology; **India is the second-largest green bond market**, and **Ghaziabad Municipal Corporation became the first Municipal Corporation to raise ₹150 crore from a green bond in 2021**. **Social bonds** finance **socially impactful projects** related to concerns such as human rights, equality and animal welfare — 'vaccine bonds' are social bonds. **Sustainability-linked bonds** are a **combination of green and social bonds**; their **proceeds are not meant for a specific project but for general corporate purposes to achieve Key Performance Indicators**; **UltraTech Cement raised US$400 million through India's first sustainability-linked bonds in 2021**, aiming to cut carbon emissions over the bond's ten-year life.

**Euro issues by Indian companies.** Indian companies may raise foreign currency resources by issuing **ordinary equity shares through GDRs or ADRs and/or Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds (FCCB)** to foreign investors including NRIs residing abroad; such investment is treated as **Foreign Direct Investment**, governed by the **Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds and Ordinary Shares (through depositary receipt mechanism) Scheme, 1993** and later notifications. **ADRs** are securities offered by **non-US companies wanting to list on a US exchange**, each ADR representing a certain number of the company's regular shares, letting US investors buy shares without the costs of investing directly on a foreign exchange. Indian companies have **preferred GDRs to ADRs** because the US market imposes higher responsibility in disclosure, costs, liabilities and timing, the most onerous aspect being **full, half-yearly and quarterly accounts in accordance with, or reconciled with, US GAAP**. **GDRs** are **negotiable certificates held in the bank of one country representing a specific number of shares of a stock traded on the exchange of another country**, used to raise capital in **dollars or euros**, mainly traded in European countries and particularly in London. **Infosys Technologies was the first Indian company listed on Nasdaq in 1999**; **Reliance Industries Limited was the first Indian firm to issue a sponsored GDR or ADR**. ==**Indian Depository Receipts (IDRs)** apply the depository receipt mechanism in the Indian capital market: **foreign companies can issue IDRs to raise funds from the Indian capital market on the same lines as an Indian company uses ADRs/GDRs to raise foreign capital**, and IDRs are **listed and traded in India in the same way as other Indian securities**.==

**Contemporary sources of funding (§10).** ==**Crowd funding** means **raising money for an individual or organisation from a group of people to fund a project, typically via the internet** (social media and crowdfunding websites).== It generally involves collecting funds from **family, friends, strangers, corporates and many more, in exchange for equity (equity funding), loans (P2P lending) or nothing at all (donation)**. It also **helps a start-up to substantiate demand for its product before entering into production**. **Three parties are involved: the fund raiser, the mediator and the fund investor**; the platforms (mediator) may charge a **processing fee, transaction fee etc., as a fixed amount, a percentage or a combination**.

**Equity funding** — equity crowdfunding is a mechanism where the **investor invests money in an organisation and receives securities of that organisation in return**, each investor being entitled to a stake depending on the investment; the **digital nature targets a large number of investors with small contributions** and it is **mostly adopted by start-ups**. **Peer-to-Peer (P2P) lending** — ==**that category of crowdfunding where lenders match with borrowers to provide unsecured loans through an online platform**==; the funds raised are **paid back with interest**, though this lending involves a **risk of default** just as banks bear in conventional lending; investors can visit P2P platforms and choose amongst borrowers considering risk and returns. **Start-up funding** — a start-up finds it difficult to manage bank loans, leaving crowdfunding as one of its sources; it may take the form of equity funding, P2P lending or both. **Donation-based crowdfunding** — a large group of people **donate money as charity for a cause with no expectation of any ownership or debt**.
So **crowd funding is the broader concept and P2P lending is basically a part of crowd funding**.

answer_points: **ESG bonds** carry a responsibility of the issuer company to prioritise optimal environmental, social and governance factors. Investing in ESG bonds is considered socially responsible investing.

official_questions.question: Explain the following international financial instruments: (i) fully hedged bonds, (ii) medium term notes, (iii) floating rate notes, (iv) Euro commercial papers.
answer_points: **Fully hedged bonds:** in foreign bonds the risk of currency fluctuations exists; fully hedged bonds eliminate the risk by selling in forward markets the entire stream of principal and interest payments.

**Medium Term Notes (MTN):** certain issuers need frequent financing through the bond route, including the Euro bond, but frequent issues may be costly and ineffective. Instead, investors can follow the MTN programme, under which several lots of bonds can be issued, all having different features, e.g. different coupon rates and different currencies. The timing of each lot can be decided keeping in mind future market opportunities, and the entire documentation and regulatory approvals can be taken at one point of time.
**Floating Rate Notes (FRN):** these are issued up to seven years maturity; interest rates are adjusted to reflect the prevailing exchange rates, and they provide cheaper money than foreign loans.
**Euro Commercial Papers (ECP):** ECPs are short-term money market instruments with a maturity period of less than one year, usually designated in US dollars.
official_questions.conclusion: One mark per instrument; the numbers (seven years, less than one year) matter.

Foreign companies can issue IDRs to raise funds from the Indian market on the same lines as an Indian company uses ADRs or GDRs to raise foreign capital.
The IDRs are listed and traded in India in the same way as other Indian securities are traded.

The issue proceeds can also be used to fund a company's local opportunities.

official_questions.question: Explain the features of crowd funding.
answer_points: Crowdfunding means raising money for an individual or organisation from a group of people to fund a project, typically via the internet (social media and crowdfunding websites).

It generally involves collecting funds from family, friends, strangers, corporates and many more, in exchange for equity (known as equity funding), loans (known as P2P lending) or nothing at all (i.e. donation).
This source of funding also helps a start-up to substantiate demand for its product before entering into production.

In the crowdfunding process, three parties are involved: the fund raiser, the mediator and the fund investor. The platforms (mediator) may charge certain fees in the form of a processing fee, transaction fee etc., either as a fixed amount, a percentage, or a combination of both.
official_questions.conclusion: Four points; the three-party structure is the distinguishing detail.
keywords: fund raiser, mediator and fund investor

official_questions.question: Distinguish between crowd funding and Peer-to-Peer (P2P) lending.
answer_points: **Crowd funding:** raising money for an individual or organisation from a group of people to fund a project, typically via the internet. It generally involves collecting funds from family, friends, strangers, corporates and many more, in exchange for equity (equity funding), loans (P2P lending) or nothing at all (donation). It also helps a start-up substantiate demand for its product before entering into production.
**Peer-to-Peer (P2P) lending:** that category of crowdfunding where lenders match with borrowers in order to provide unsecured loans through an online platform.
The funds raised are paid back by the borrowers with interest, though this kind of lending involves a certain risk of default, just as banks bear in the case of the conventional method of lending.
Anyone interested in investing money under P2P lending can visit the P2P lending platforms and choose amongst borrowers considering risk and returns.
Hence crowd funding is a broader concept and P2P lending is basically a part of crowd funding.
official_questions.conclusion: The closing line — P2P is a part of crowd funding, not an alternative — is the marker of a complete answer.

expected_questions.question: Explain External Commercial Borrowings, stating the recognised sources and the two routes under which they can be accessed.
answer_points: ECBs refer to commercial loans — in the form of bank loans, buyers' credit, suppliers' credit and securitised instruments such as floating rate notes and fixed rate bonds — availed from non-resident lenders with a minimum average maturity of 3 years.

Borrowers can raise ECBs through internationally recognised sources: international banks, international capital markets, multilateral financial institutions such as IFC and ADB, export credit agencies, suppliers of equipment, foreign collaborators and foreign equity holders.

ECBs can be accessed under two routes: the Automatic route and the Approval route. Under the Automatic route there is no need to take RBI or Government approval, whereas such approval is necessary under the Approval route.

Companies registered under the Companies Act and NGOs engaged in micro-finance activities are eligible for the Automatic route; financial institutions and banks dealing exclusively in infrastructure or export finance, and those which participated in the textile and steel sector restructuring packages approved by the government, are required to take the Approval route.

expected_questions.question: Explain equity funding, start-up funding and donation-based crowdfunding as contemporary sources of funding.
answer_points: **Equity funding:** equity crowdfunding is a mechanism where an investor invests money in an organisation and receives securities of that organisation in return. Every investor is entitled to a stake in the organisation depending on the investment. The digital nature of crowdfunding targets a large number of investors with small contributions, and this type of funding is mostly adopted by start-ups.

**Start-up funding:** a start-up company, being newly formed, needs funds before starting any project, but as a start-up it is difficult to manage loans from banks, leaving crowdfunding as one of the sources of finance. Through crowdfunding a start-up can raise money from a large group of people, in the form of equity funding, P2P lending or both.
**Donation-based crowdfunding:** a source of finance where a large group of people donate money as charity for some cause with no expectation of any ownership or debt.

In all three, the three parties of the crowdfunding process — the fund raiser, the mediator (platform) and the fund investor — remain the same, and the platform may charge a processing or transaction fee.
keywords: no expectation of any ownership or debt

cases.title: Integrated Case 1 — Meghna Exports Ltd. raises money on every front
facts: Meghna Exports Ltd. is setting up a new processing unit. A financial institution has sanctioned a ₹60 crore term loan, but disbursement will take four months. To avoid losing the building season, Meghna borrows ₹12 crore from its bank for that period, hypothecating movable assets and giving a demand promissory note; the rate is higher than the term-loan rate and the loan will be adjusted when the institution disburses.

For the equipment, Meghna does not buy outright. A leasing company purchases the machine, borrowing 80% of the cost from a bank, and leases it to Meghna. Meghna pays the rentals directly to that bank, and the surplus over the bank's dues goes to the leasing company, which claims the depreciation allowance.

Meghna has a confirmed export order backed by an irrevocable letter of credit. Its bank advances funds so that it can buy raw material, process, pack and ship the consignment; the advance must be squared off within 180 days by negotiating the export bills.

After shipment, the proceeds are still to be realised, so the bank discounts the usance export bills backed by bills of lading, and separately advances against duty drawback receivable on export performance — an advance of a clean nature.
